name: Horizontal stripes and layering for width

lead: People wear horizontal stripes and stacked layers to make the chest and shoulders look wider and the upper body bulkier, with the effect visible as soon as the outfit is on.

Layers add real fabric volume around the torso, and horizontal patterns are said to lead the eye sideways across the body. No direct studies of stripes or layering on perceived body width were found; related illusion research uses line drawings, not clothing.

paras: People choose horizontally striped tops, thicker knits, and layered shirts, tees and jackets, often on slimmer frames wanting more upper-body presence. The effect is immediate and works with any wardrobe.
No health risks apply. Heavy layering can add bulk at the waist as well as the chest, and in hot weather it can be uncomfortable.

angle.text: People wear horizontal stripes and layers to look broader across the chest and shoulders; layers add real volume and stripes are said to draw the eye sideways. The effect is immediate with clothing alone. No direct studies were found.

lead: Horizontal stripes and layering are clothing techniques that people in looksmaxxing communities use to make the upper body look broader or bulkier. Layered garments add real volume, and horizontal patterns are said to draw the eye sideways across the chest and shoulders.

Searching for supporting research found nothing specific to this practice. The related perceptual literature on the vertical-horizontal illusion concerns line judgments, not clothing, and no clinical studies of stripes or layering on perceived body width were found [1].
infobox: Visual bulk and apparent upper-body width

paras: Practitioners describe two ideas: that horizontal stripes make a torso read as wider, and that layering (for example a jacket over a sweater over a shirt) adds bulk where the wearer is slim. The wiki found no source documenting the origin of either idea in looksmaxxing culture.

Research on the vertical-horizontal illusion finds that observers tend to judge a vertical line as longer than an equal horizontal line, an effect that persists even when people know the lines match [1]. This work involves simple line figures and does not address clothing stripes or body size, so it does not directly test the claim.
